reels.title: A dinner plate from 1616

prediction.prompt: In 1616 Dirk Hartog nailed a pewter plate to a post on an island off western Australia. When did the next European find it?

frames.text: On 25 October 1616, Dirk Hartog reached an island off western Australia. This is the pewter plate he left there.
frames.say: On the twenty-fifth of October, sixteen sixteen, Dirk Hartog reached an island off western Australia. This is the pewter plate he left there.

frames.text: He landed at Cape Inscription, the island's northern tip, and nailed the plate to a post on the cliff top.
In 1697 another Dutch captain, Willem de Vlamingh, came ashore and found it.
frames.say: In sixteen ninety-seven another Dutch captain, Willem de Vlahming, came ashore and found it.

frames.text: He put up a new plate, and the original went back to the Netherlands. It is now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
It is the oldest known surviving object from European exploration of Australia. The island, Wirruwana to the Malgana people, now bears Hartog's name.
frames.say: It is the oldest known surviving object from European exploration of Australia. The island, Wirroo-wahna to the Malgana people, now bears Hartog's name.

reels.takeaway: Hartog's plate marked his landing in 1616. Willem de Vlamingh removed it in 1697, and it is now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

claims.quote: On 25 October 1616, he landed at Cape Inscription on the very northernmost tip of Dirk Hartog Island, in Shark Bay.

claims.claim: Vlamingh replaced it with his own plate copying Hartog's inscription; the original was returned to the Netherlands and is kept in the Rijksmuseum Amsterdam

reels.title: The frond in Charnwood Forest

prediction.prompt: In 1957 schoolboys found a fossil frond in England. How could scientists be sure it was older than the Cambrian?

choices.label: Geological maps of the rocks it lay in
It looked unlike any living thing

frames.text: A museum model of Ediacaran life, crowded with feathery fronds, many of them Charnia.
Living things like these first appeared about 600 million years ago, and lasted until the Cambrian.
In 1956 a 15-year-old, Tina Negus, found a fossil frond in Charnwood Forest, England. She was not believed.
frames.say: In nineteen fifty-six a fifteen-year-old, Tina Neegus, found a fossil frond in Charnwood Forest, England. She was not believed.

frames.text: A year later, three schoolboys found it again. One of them, Roger Mason, was also 15.
No one could doubt the rock's age. The British Geological Survey had mapped it in detail, and it was Precambrian.
After Charnia, scientists finally took seriously the idea of life before the Cambrian.

reels.takeaway: Teenagers found Charnia in rock that geologists had mapped as Precambrian. It made scientists take life before the Cambrian seriously.
